by.claim: The CI diff failures reporting that user system:serviceaccount:argocd:argocd-server is attempting to grant RBAC permissions not currently held are the Kubernetes escalation-prevention check firing against the identity performing the server-side apply dry-run, and they appeared in projects that had just enabled the sync impersonation flag. The impersonation design routes the sync operation through the AppProject's destinationServiceAccounts while leaving the diff path on its own identity, so the identity the check is evaluated against on the diff surface is not the identity that performs the actual apply. A ClusterRole the diff surface reports as forbidden can still be applied by the sync path when the mapped service account holds those grants, which means the diff output is not evidence of what the sync is authorized to do, in either direction.

Server-Side Diff runs as the cluster credential from the cluster Secret and, because Kubernetes RBAC has no dry-run verb, requires real patch authority on every resource kind an Application ships, growing by one kind per new chart with no end state. That reassembles on the standing cluster credential exactly the concentration of privilege the impersonation proposal exists to remove: its stated premise is that the control plane must otherwise be granted the highest privilege any tenant needs, creating a large attack surface where compromising Argo CD yields cluster-wide write. Enabling destinationServiceAccounts does not shrink it, since the diff path ignores that mapping, so whoever obtains the cluster Secret holds write authority on every kind in the external cluster, protected only by Argo CD's convention of sending dryRun=All rather than by any enforced boundary.

Nothing on the hydrated branch records who pushed a commit. The hydrator design copies commitAuthor forward from the dry commit into the README and hydrator.metadata, and every push is made by the GitHub App credential in the repository-write Secret, never by the person named in that field; the signing feature that would tie a commit to a key defaults to commitserver.sign.hydrated.commits false. So a holder of the repository-write credential can push a hydrated commit attributed in metadata to any dry-commit author, and the evidence a reviewer would consult (git history plus hydrator.metadata) reproduces the attacker's chosen attribution rather than contradicting it. Detection of such a push depends on an opt-in that is off by default.

The History and Rollback design pushes to the sync branch outside the commit server, and the commit server is the only component that holds the signing key, mounted from the Secret in the Argo CD namespace. The consequence is that the check actually deciding whether a rollback lands is the git host enforcing the branch's SourceIntegrity policy, not Argo CD: the rollback push is unsigned and is rejected there, while the UI shows only a failed push with no messaging tying it back to signing and no retry path. Where SourceIntegrity is not configured on the sync branch, the same reasoning removes the only enforcement, and any holder of write access to that branch can place manifests on it that Argo CD will sync with no commit-server record of the push.

distractorGate.note: DX1/DX2 violations fail rung 3 for runs scored from this date; score files recorded earlier are never regenerated and keep their as-run results. Evidence: five distractor-disciplined runs (two single-pass, three composed dispatch-shape) all clean; every run before the discipline paragraph violated at least one.
